rows.title: Ex-dividend entitlement is determined before the ex-date, not by payment-day ownership
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: A regular $0.40 cash dividend has a Tuesday ex-date and a Friday payable date. A buyer acquiring 50 shares on Monday (before ex-date) is eligible for 50 × $0.40 = $20 before taxes; a Tuesday buyer is not eligible for that declared dividend.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Large special dividends, stock distributions, market holidays and due bills can change conventional schedules. Eligibility says nothing about total investm
rows.sourceFactScope: SEC Investor.gov ex-date rule; 25%-or-more special dividends exception

rows.title: Cash dividends and share-price changes must both enter a holding-period return
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: Buy at $40.00, sell at $39.00 and receive $1.50 cash dividend per share. Total price-plus-cash return = (39 − 40 + 1.50)/40 = 1.25%, although price alone fell 2.50%.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: The calculation omits transaction costs, taxes, reinvestment dates and any corporate actions; ex-date adjustments alone are not a free return.
rows.sourceFactScope: Investor.gov states investment return can arise from changes in asset value or dividend and interest payments; the ex-dividend eligibility reference does not on its own establish total investment return or price-only performance. Fictional price-plus-cash math still needs independent review.

internalScopeVerification.basis: current SEC Investor.gov publicly accessible source article, reviewed for claim-specific scope

rows.title: Indicated dividend yield uses a changing quote and a non-guaranteed payout assumption
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: A company recently declares $0.30 quarterly. If four identical payments continued, the indicated annual amount would be $1.20. At $24.00 a share the indicated yield would be 1.20/24 = 5.00%, not an assured 5% future return.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Management may reduce, suspend or change dividends; market price, taxes and nonstandard distributions change comparisons.
rows.sourceFactScope: FINRA investor education defines dividend yield as annual dividend divided by current price; yield changes with share price or dividend rate. Original $0.30 x 4 / $24 = 5% is a conditional illustration, not an assured payment, return or investment advice. Individual editorial, full reference/math and publication rights acceptance remain on HOLD.

rows.title: A share repurchase and a cash dividend distribute value through different mechanisms
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: A company has 1,000 shares and buys back 100 at $10 each for $1,000. If retired with no new shares, outstanding shares become 900; an unchanged holder with 90 shares moves from 9.00% to 10.00% ownership, but receives no dividend cash from that repurchase.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Non-selling shareholders receive no direct repurchase cash. Retired shares, treasury treatment, dilution, issuer value, taxes and repurchase price affect outcomes. Do not present the vacated 2023 disclosure rule as currently binding.
rows.sourceFactScope: The SEC's archived 2023 Commissioner speech supplies historical policy discussion, not current regulation. The SEC March 2024 notice confirms the rule amendments were vacated effective December 19, 2023. Original 90/1000 to 90/900 math is conditional on actual cancellation and no issuance.

rows.title: Preferred dividends and common voting claims are different security rights
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: An issuer has common and noncumulative preferred stock with a contractual $2 preferred annual dividend. If no dividend is declared in one year, the student cannot assume a $2 arrear later; cumulative terms would be required for that conclusion.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Preferred shares are not risk-free bonds and liquidation preferences may be worth less when company assets are insufficient.
rows.sourceFactScope: SEC Investor.gov stocks FAQ explains priority of preferred relative to common; noncumulative dividend contract exceptions still require exact prospectus.

rows.title: Primary shares raise issuer capital while secondary-market sales transfer existing ownership
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: Issuer A sells 1,000 newly issued shares at $10 for $10,000 gross before offering expenses. Two days later an owner resells 100 of those shares for $12 each; the $1,200 gross goes to that seller, not as another $1,200 capital raise for Issuer A.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Underwriting expenses, selling shareholder secondary offerings and unusual structures can change who receives proceeds.
rows.sourceFactScope: Investor.gov IPO bulletin directly distinguishes new shares sold by an issuer (capital raised by company) from registered existing selling shareholders whose proceeds belong to those shareholders. Normal secondary trades similarly transfer ownership rather than new issue proceeds; keep IPO registration distinctions clear.

rows.title: An IPO offering allocation price is not the first public secondary-market trade
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: A company offers shares at $18 in a hypothetical IPO. A member not allocated shares sees a first reported public trade at $22. A $4 difference describes a comparison between two different events, not a profit available to every investor.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Allocation is limited; opening indications, opening auctions, spreads and price volatility may differ from the public first print.
rows.sourceFactScope: SEC Investor.gov IPO bulletin explains allocation, flipping and post-offering public trading; hypothetical offer/first-trade spread is arithmetic, not guaranteed allocation.

rows.title: A bond coupon rate applies to face value, not the bond's fluctuating market quote
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: $1,000 face bond with 6% annual fixed coupon promises $60 annual interest, typically $30 per semiannual payment, subject to issuer payment and stated terms; purchasing the bond at $950 would not turn the annual coupon into $57.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Actual accrued interest, principal changes, callable issues and default risk can change cash flows; coupon is not total return.
rows.sourceFactScope: Investor.gov What Are Corporate Bonds lists par (face value), coupon rate, price, maturity and yield; coupon cash must be computed from stated par and annualized coupon convention. No guaranteed secondary-market return.

internalScopeVerification.basis: public Investor.gov primary education page reviewed

rows.title: Bond current yield is annual coupon cash divided by today's market price
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: A $1,000-face 5% bond pays $50 yearly. If the clean market price is $800, simplified current yield is 50/800 = 6.25%; this does not calculate its yield to maturity.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Accrued interest, fees, reinvestment, call features, remaining term and expected return of par are omitted.
rows.sourceFactScope: SEC Investor.gov current-yield glossary confirms annual coupon / market price; distinct from yield to maturity.

rows.title: For a fixed-cash-flow bond, market price and required yield generally move oppositely
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: A one-year zero-coupon $1,000 payment is worth 1000/1.05 = $952.38 at 5% and 1000/1.10 = $909.09 at 10%. Higher required yield produces lower present value for the unchanged payment.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Callable, floating-rate, credit-change and embedded-option securities can produce more complicated price behavior.
rows.sourceFactScope: SEC Investor.gov fixed-income bulletin confirms inverse market rates and fixed-bond prices, ceteris paribus.

rows.title: A bond's premium or discount is measured against contractual par, not annual coupon
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: A $1,000 par bond is quoted at 103% of par, or $1,030 clean price: $30 premium. A quote of 97 means $970: $30 discount. Neither quote says its contractual coupon rate.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Quoted price may exclude accrued interest; callable terms or default can prevent simple par recovery.
rows.sourceFactScope: Investor.gov corporate-bond bulletin expressly shows 90% and 110% of $1,000 face-value examples for discounts and premiums. Quote convention, accrued interest and issuer call/default remain separate.

internalScopeVerification.basis: public Investor.gov primary education page reviewed

rows.title: Issuer credit risk and market interest-rate sensitivity are separate bond exposures
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: A contractual $1,000 one-year payment valued at $952.38 at 5% becomes $909.09 at 10% under unchanged promised payment assumptions. Separately, if repayment were only $900 certain at 5%, its illustrative PV would be $857.14. These are different hypothetical changes.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Real markets combine uncertain probabilities, recovery rates, liquidity, taxes and rate changes; neither demonstration is a complete pricing model.
rows.sourceFactScope: Investor.gov Bonds FAQ separately identifies credit/default risk and interest-rate price risk. Do not present issuer default and market-yield sensitivity as the same risk or assert a guaranteed bond resale price.

internalScopeVerification.basis: current SEC Investor.gov publicly accessible source article, reviewed for claim-specific scope

rows.title: An ETF's market trading price can differ from its per-share net asset value
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: Fund has $9.8 million assets, $0.2 million liabilities and 400,000 shares: NAV = $9.6m/400k = $24.00. A market print at $24.12 is a $0.12 or 0.50% premium to that illustrative NAV.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Published NAV may be calculated at end of day while a trade occurs intraday; stale valuations and market closure matter.
rows.sourceFactScope: SEC Investor.gov ETF explainer confirms traded ETF price can differ from daily NAV; hypothetical 0.5% premium remains separately computed.

rows.title: Index return and fund return can diverge without disproving an index strategy
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: A benchmark total return is +8.0% and a comparable fund total return is +7.6% over the same year. Tracking difference = 7.6% − 8.0% = −0.4 percentage points. This is one-period difference, not a time-series tracking-error standard deviation.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Share-class expenses and index methodology can change comparisons; one year does not prove long-run replication quality.
rows.sourceFactScope: Investor.gov Index Funds explicitly describes tracking error, replication differences, fund fees and trading costs; citing it does not establish a specific fund tracking-difference number.

internalScopeVerification.basis: public Investor.gov primary education page reviewed

rows.title: SIPC brokerage-custody protection is not insurance against a falling investment price
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: A share bought for $50 falls in market value to $20 while the brokerage continues operating. The $30 price decline is market loss, not a $30 SIPC claim; a separate hypothetical failure with missing shares raises a custody question.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Coverage limits and exclusions depend on account status and loss type; no assumed payout follows from a sample price change.
rows.sourceFactScope: Investor.gov SIPC excluded market-price losses

rows.title: SIPC coverage limits are claims constraints, not a substitute for brokerage reconciliation
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: A qualifying member failure leaves an illustrative missing $300,000 of eligible securities and $50,000 eligible cash for a single customer. The combined $350,000 is below the published $500,000 overall headline and cash below $250,000, but this arithmetic alone is not an entitlement finding.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Net equity calculation, property recovery, exclusions and multiple-account categories can materially affect an actual claim.
rows.sourceFactScope: Investor.gov SIPC $500000 combined/$250000 cash ceilings

rows.title: Common shareholders' residual ownership is not a creditor claim
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: Liquidation yields $700,000 assets against $800,000 enforceable senior claims. A simple model leaves $0 for common shares, rather than the negative $100,000 becoming an automatic personal bill to fully paid common holders.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Real liquidation priorities, subordinated debt and preferred terms are more complex than a two-line classroom waterfall.
rows.sourceFactScope: SEC Investor.gov public-company bankruptcy glossary places common equity after creditors; no negative common-equity payout inferred.

rows.title: Traditional open-end mutual fund transactions and ETF intraday trades use different price mechanisms
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: A classroom open-end mutual fund receives a properly timed order and calculates a next NAV of $15.20; an illustrative ETF quote at $15.25 during the day is a tradable indication subject to execution, not the fund's final NAV.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Fund restrictions, market closures, premiums, discounts and delayed valuation can invalidate straightforward same-day comparisons.
rows.sourceFactScope: Investor.gov mutual-fund/ETF characteristics directly compares daily mutual-fund NAV transactions with intraday ETF market-price transactions; no guaranteed ETF fill or NAV equality.

internalScopeVerification.basis: public Investor.gov primary education page reviewed

rows.title: A bond's stated maturity and its sensitivity to yield changes are different measurements
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: Two securities each mature in five years, but one pays annual coupons and one pays no coupon. Their principal dates match; the coupon bond returns some cash earlier, so their Macaulay durations need not match five years.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Yield curve shocks, embedded options and changing cash-flow assumptions can defeat simple duration approximations.
rows.sourceFactScope: FINRA Duration investor source directly distinguishes Macaulay/modified/effective duration and sensitivity to market rate changes. Maturity is contractual principal repayment date, duration a rate sensitivity/cash-flow timing measure; do not infer guaranteed realized holding-period loss.

rows.title: Unrealized quote gains and realized sale gains are different accounting events
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: Ten shares purchased at $20 show a last price of $23. Unrealized gross difference is 10 × ($23 − $20) = $30; absent a completed sale it is not $30 of received sale cash.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Tax basis adjustments, partial lots, transaction costs, currency and distributions may change a real realized result.
rows.sourceFactScope: SEC Investor.gov capital gain glossary requires sale for realized capital gain; displayed mark-to-market gain is unrealized.

rows.title: Reinvesting fund cash distributions changes share count, not guaranteed profit
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: 100 eligible fund units × $0.30 cash each = $30; a $15 reinvestment price buys 2 more units, leaving 102 units before costs. The $30 was part of the distribution, not free extra profit.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Distribution classifications, reinvestment prices and share fractions vary; cash payouts often reduce NAV and taxes may arise even without receiving cash.
rows.sourceFactScope: SEC Investor.gov fund distributions bulletin confirms reinvestment purchases additional shares; distribution is not guaranteed added wealth.

rows.title: Consecutive holding-period returns must be compounded in sequence
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: $100 earns +10% to $110, then loses 10% of $110, ending $99. Full-period return = 1.10×0.90−1 = −1%, not zero.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Contributions, withdrawals, distributions and valuation gaps change the account-return calculation, and observed historical percentages do not forecast lat
rows.sourceFactScope: FINRA investor education explains compounded multi-period returns and why simple averaging can misstate performance; original fictional $100 x 1.10 x 0.90 = $99 (-1%) and independent $200 x 1.20 x 0.75 = $180 (-10%) must be interpreted as no-external-flow illustrations only. Publication rights and independent acceptance remain on HOLD.

internalScopeVerification.basis: Current public FINRA investor-education page reviewed for period return compounding, November 3, 2026

rows.title: Arithmetic average return and geometric compounded growth are different statistics
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: Annual +20% and −10% give arithmetic average (20−10)/2=5%. The factor is 1.2×0.9=1.08, and geometric average sqrt(1.08)−1≈3.92%.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Unequal intervals, external cash flows, and a terminal gross factor of zero change or limit the standard interpretation.
rows.sourceFactScope: FINRA return bulletin differentiates total and annualized rate of return and provides a multi-year example, but does not independently establish arithmetic-mean versus geometric-mean definitions for a specified return series. Preserve independently tested fictional factors and obtain direct time-series statistics source.

rows.title: Real purchasing-power return is calculated from ratios of nominal and inflation factors
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: An 8% nominal gain with 3% matched inflation produces 1.08/1.03−1=4.854% real return, about 4.85%; simple 8−3=5% is only an approximation.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Personal consumption baskets, taxes and mismatched CPI periods make this a model of purchasing power, not a personal household guarantee.
rows.sourceFactScope: BLS verifies properly aligned CPI index percent-change computation and base-period comparability. It is not direct evidence for the exact real investment return equation (1+nominal)/(1+inflation)-1; that equation must be independently sourced/proved, with same-period aligned inputs.

rows.title: Annualizing a partial-year outcome does not establish an earned twelve-month return
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: Exactly six months return +5% with no flows; under repeated equal-half-year compounding, annualized equivalent = 1.05²−1=10.25%, but only 5% has been observed.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Short periods are highly sensitive to timing, volatility, fees and hypothetical reinvestment; extrapolation is not a credible trading forecast.
rows.sourceFactScope: FINRA return bulletin differentiates multi-year realized holding-period return and calculated annualized rate. Applying a mathematical annualization factor to partial-period results is a comparison convention, not a realized 12-month investment result or forecast; no extra claim of payout certainty.

rows.title: Simple portfolio period return uses the opening asset weights
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: A $1,000 account starts 60% Fund A, 40% Fund B; returns +10% and −5%. Combined = 0.6×10%+0.4×(−5%)=+4%, ending at $1,040.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Rebalancing, leverage, cash flows, tax lots and noncomparable dates require more sophisticated performance treatment.
rows.sourceFactScope: SEC Investor.gov asset-allocation publication supports beginning exposure mix but does not itself verify hypothetical 60/40 return arithmetic.

rows.title: Portfolio allocations drift when different holdings change market value
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: $600 stocks grow 20% to $720; $400 bonds stay unchanged. Total $1,120; stock share becomes $720/$1,120=64.29%, not 60%.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Fees, cash movement, splits and multiple holdings complicate real weights; the resulting allocation says nothing about expected return.
rows.sourceFactScope: Investor.gov rebalancing explainer states differing asset returns cause allocation drift; individual original arithmetic must still define as-of holdings and denominator.

internalScopeVerification.basis: public Investor.gov primary education page reviewed

rows.title: Asset rebalancing targets apply to current total account value
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: Current stocks $720, bonds $400, combined $1,120. For a hypothetical 60/40 target stocks should be $672 and bonds $448; an idealized transfer would move $48 between categories.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Transaction fees, account restrictions, liquidity and taxes may prevent exact shifts, so arithmetic is not advice to place those orders.
rows.sourceFactScope: Investor.gov Rebalancing definition directly supports returning to the original allocation mix; current-dollar target multiplication is independently original fictional arithmetic, not a quoted statutory formula.

internalScopeVerification.basis: public Investor.gov primary education page reviewed

rows.title: A squared-weight concentration index does not measure return covariance
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: 50%,30%,20% weights give 0.50²+0.30²+0.20²=0.38; equal thirds would give 1/3≈0.333, showing greater concentration by this measure.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: HHI of portfolio weights describes concentration, not covariance, future loss, suitability or guaranteed diversification benefits; neither this decimal-weight index nor its reciprocal is an antitrust compliance finding.
rows.sourceFactScope: State Street explicitly explains portfolio HHI as sum of squared weights and effective holdings as its reciprocal; the fictional .38 calculation remains original. This does not establish covariance, market risks or licensing rights.

rows.title: Holding multiple securities does not prevent simultaneous portfolio losses
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: Two different stocks each have a 50% allocation. If both fall 10%, portfolio change = 0.5×(−10%)+0.5×(−10%)=−10%. Number of tickers does not remove the shared decline.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: This is one fictional scenario, not a measured correlation or loss-frequency estimate; future co-movement remains uncertain.
rows.sourceFactScope: SEC Investor.gov diversification source explains common exposed risk is possible across different holdings; numeric shock independently checked.

rows.title: An unaudited quarterly 10-Q and audited annual 10-K cover different periods
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: Issuer reports 2025 audited annual sales $100m, then 2026 first-quarter unaudited sales $24m. The quarter is not full-year 2026 revenue; multiplying by four does not create audited annual evidence.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Acquisitions, seasonal demand, revisions and year-to-date conventions can break naive extrapolation.
rows.sourceFactScope: Investor.gov Form 10-Q glossary says unaudited quarterly statements for first three fiscal quarters; EDGAR investor guide separately identifies audited 10-K statements.

internalScopeVerification.basis: public Investor.gov primary education page reviewed

rows.title: An 8-K agreement announcement is not necessarily a completed cash transaction
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: A current report describes a signed conditional $15m asset-sale agreement. The classroom cannot report $15m received or realized profit until the relevant completion and accounting evidence is available.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Different events trigger different disclosure requirements; legal and accounting impacts are fact-specific.
rows.sourceFactScope: Investor.gov How to Read an 8-K distinguishes Item 1.01 agreement entry from Item 2.01 completion of acquisition or asset disposition. An announced agreement alone does not prove closing.

internalScopeVerification.basis: public Investor.gov primary education page reviewed

rows.title: Fiscal statement dates are not equivalent to historical public-information timestamps
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: A company's fiscal year ends December 31. A Form 10-K is accepted by EDGAR February 20 at 14:00; public dissemination may occur later than acceptance; the first separately verified public observation is February 20 at 14:03. A January 15 or February 20 14:01 replay cannot use that filing. Any earlier press release needs its own documented time.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: SEC does not record the exact second of first SEC.gov visibility, and 1–3 minutes is not a guaranteed bound. A reported public observation is a distinct, source-specific event, not an official SEC availability stamp.
rows.sourceFactScope: SEC Webmaster FAQ: EDGAR acceptance and publication differ. Filings often appear 1–3 minutes later, but no guaranteed maximum or exact first-available timestamp exists. A 14:03 classroom retrieval is only an independently verified hypothetical observation.

rows.title: Operating margin accounts for operating expenses beyond direct cost of sales
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: Annual revenue $100m minus COGS $60m gives gross $40m; subtract $30m operating expenses gives operating income $10m and operating margin 10%, not gross margin 40%.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Presentation of unusual costs, segments and non-GAAP adjustments varies; margin alone cannot establish cash generation.
rows.sourceFactScope: SEC operating-margin income-from-operations/net revenue

rows.title: EBIT interest coverage compares same-period earnings and interest expense
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: EBIT $12m and annual interest expense $3m imply a simple coverage ratio 12/3=4.0×; it is not four years of cash on hand.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Debt covenants, refinancing, noncash income and changing rates make the coverage multiple insufficient to predict future payment.
rows.sourceFactScope: Damodaran Stern NYU financial ratios table explicitly defines interest coverage as EBIT divided by interest expense. Denominator zero/negative, reporting period and definitions of expense remain separate editorial/arithmetical checks; no interest payment guarantee.
rows.sourceReconciliationNote: Damodaran directly defines interest coverage as EBIT/interest expense; example 12/3=4x, no liquidity guarantee.

rows.title: Inventory turnover uses cost of sales divided by matched average inventory
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: Yearly COGS $120m; inventory opens $20m and closes $30m. Average = $25m; turnover = $120m/$25m=4.8 times that year.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Seasonality, product write-downs and inventory accounting conventions make cross-company turnover comparison conditional.
rows.sourceFactScope: SEC COGS/average beginning-and-ending inventory

rows.title: Days sales outstanding is an estimated collection cycle rather than an invoice due date
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: Annual credit sales $180m and average trade receivables $18m yield 18/180×365 = 36.5 days, a portfolio-level collection estimate.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Receivable quality, write-offs, seasonal sales, cash-sales inclusion and different 360/365 day bases can alter the result.
rows.sourceFactScope: SEC financial-statement beginner guide explains receivables/statement concepts but does NOT specify days-sales-outstanding using matched credit sales, average receivables and a defined period length. Seek direct accounting formula and note provider numerator conventions.

rows.title: Return on equity needs comparable attributable income and average book equity
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: Attributable earnings $15m; book common equity rises from $80m to $120m. Average $100m; ROE = 15/100 = 15%, without saying stockholders earned a 15% market return.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Negative equity, buybacks and extraordinary items can distort interpretation; peer comparisons require accounting consistency.
rows.sourceFactScope: Damodaran NYU Stern ROE definition states net income divided by book equity and says equity denominator can use the period's beginning or average value. The attributable-income numerator, preferred/noncontrolling adjustments and negative/zero equity are explicit limitations.

rows.title: Debt-to-equity ratios change when the numerator defines debt differently
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: Interest-bearing debt is $90m and book equity $60m on one date: 90/60=1.5×. Total-liabilities-to-equity could be different if it includes trade payables.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Negative book equity, off-balance commitments and financial-sector accounting can make conventional ratios misleading.
rows.sourceFactScope: SEC debt-equity illustration uses total liabilities / equity; distinct from financial debt only
rows.sourceReconciliationNote: SEC financial guide defines total liabilities/equity, a DIFFERENT numerator from interest-bearing debt/equity in this guide.

rows.title: Earnings yield is an EPS-to-price ratio, not cash paid to shareholders
rows.originalWorkedCase: FICTIONAL: Price $50, trailing EPS $5. P/E=10×; accounting earnings yield=5/50=10%. That does not entitle the owner to $5 cash or a 10% future return.
rows.originalReviewCaveat: Loss-making or zero-EPS issuers, earnings restatements and special items make ordinary P/E comparison unreliable.
rows.sourceFactScope: SEC financial-statement guide defines EPS and P/E as price per share divided by EPS, and explains that a company generally retains some earnings. For positive denominators, EPS/price is algebraically reciprocal P/E, not dividend cash paid; negative/zero EPS requires caveat.
rows.sourceReconciliationNote: SEC P/E ratio equals price/EPS; when EPS is positive, EPS/price equals reciprocal earnings yield; not paid cash.
